title: Six sets of six
hookLine: the eye is not self, forms are not self, seeing is not self

lines: THIRTY-SIX ITEMS, SIX ROWS OF SIX.
cards: Thirty-six. That's how many items the hundred and forty-eighth discourse lays out, in six rows of six, like a spreadsheet of experience.

It opens in Jeta's Grove at Savatthi with the Buddha announcing a teaching good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end. Then he simply counts. It can sound dry on the page, almost like an inventory.
But the text says that while it was being spoken, the minds of sixty monks were freed.

teach.b: Here are the six rows. The six inner bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. The six outer bases: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and things known by the mind.
Six kinds of consciousness, one for each meeting: seeing, hearing, and so on. Six kinds of contact, when sense, object and consciousness come together. Six kinds of feeling born of that contact.
Six kinds of craving born of that feeling. Then the argument, and it's short. If anyone says the eye is self, the Buddha says, that doesn't hold.
The eye's arising and passing away are plainly seen. If the eye were self, you'd have to say: my self arises and passes away. So the eye is not self.
Then he runs the same test down the whole table. Forms: not self. Eye-consciousness: not self.
Eye-contact, feeling, craving: not self. Thirty-six times, the same short proof.
The Pali word is anatta, not-self. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say nobody is here, or that nothing matters.
It says each piece you might point to and call me comes and goes, so it can't be the permanent owner you were looking for. Then the discourse turns practical.
When a pleasant feeling comes and you delight in it, a tendency toward lust lies underneath.
A painful one, resisted: aversion lies underneath. A neutral one, unnoticed: ignorance. Seeing all six rows clearly, the text says, a person grows disenchanted, and is freed.

how: The six sense bases are a standard frame for insight meditation in Theravada practice; teachers often walk students through them one at a time, asking whether anything found there is lasting or can be called self.

o: not-self: nothing in experience is a lasting self
a self that is hidden beneath the senses
the belief that no one exists at all

games.q: six sets of six: tap the pairs.
p: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind
forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, ideas

s: MN 148 teaches that nobody is here and nothing matters
it says each piece you might call 'me' comes and goes, so it can't be a permanent self.
the text says sixty monks were freed while it was spoken
the discourse closes by saying so: sixty monks freed from the taints, through not clinging.
the argument is: if the eye were self, my self would arise and pass away
since the eye's arising and passing is plain to see, the eye isn't self.

games.q: someone tells you: the eye is my self. what does the Buddha in MN 148 point to?
o: the eye arises and passes away, so the self would too.
the eye is too small to be a self.
only the mind can be a self.
games.why: he points to change: if the eye were self, you'd have to say 'my self arises and passes away', and that doesn't hold.

practice: Close your eyes and let sounds come: a car, your own breath, a hum. Look for the one who owns the hearing: there's the sound, the ear, the hearing, arising and fading; is there anything else, standing apart and permanent?
Don't argue with yourself; just look, gently.

wordCard.voice: Anatta. Not-self: thirty-six pieces of experience, each one arising and passing, so none of them the lasting self, tested row by row. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali anatta: not-self. Sanskrit anatman. tested here on thirty-six pieces of experience.

carryVoice: Your line: not self, six times. Thirty-six squares, and the same quiet answer in each. Day five hundred thirteen, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 148, Chachakka Sutta (the six sets of six)
